repos.title: Optimizing the Interface Between Knowledge Graphs and LLMs for Complex Reasoning
repos.paper_summary:
Dreamify is a hyperparameter optimization framework for Cognee, a modular system that constructs knowledge graphs and retrieves context for LLMs. It uses Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to tune six parameters: chunk size, retriever type, top-k count, QA prompt, graph extraction prompt, and task preprocessing method. The authors evaluate on filtered subsets of HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue, using 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset. Each experiment runs 50 trials, scoring configurations by exact match, F1, or DeepEval correctness.

Optimization yields consistent gains over default baselines. For example, HotPotQA exact match rises from 0.042 to 0.667, and F1 increases from 0.169 to 0.840. On the held-out test sets, performance generally remains above baseline but drops slightly compared to training scores; however, TwoWikiMultiHop F1 improves from 0.625 in training to 0.704 in testing. The paper notes that small evaluation sets introduce variability, and no single configuration performs best across all benchmarks, indicating that optimal settings are task-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hyperparameter tuning of graph-enhanced retrieval pipelines is underexamined, though many interacting settings affect multi-hop question answering.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers retrieval-augmented pipelines, three multi-hop benchmarks, graph-based question answering, and prior optimization of such pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Automated Knowledge Graph Construction: Cognee
digest_headlines.headline: Cognee is an open-source framework whose modular pipeline and built-in evaluation let the whole system serve as an optimization objective.

digest_headlines.heading: Hyperparameter Optimization Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Dreamify tunes six Cognee parameters with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, scoring each trial by a benchmark metric averaged over questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Nine experiments pair three datasets with three metrics, each running 50 trials on 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuned settings beat baselines on all nine training metrics, but most hold-out scores fell below training scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning gave consistent but uneven gains, and the authors call for custom benchmarks and better evaluation of graph-based systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes Cognee's extract-cognify-load architecture, its default pipeline stages, retriever types, and the evaluation framework.

repos.title: An Open and Comprehensive Pipeline for Unified Object Grounding and Detection
repos.paper_summary: MM-Grounding-DINO is an open-source pipeline for unified object grounding and detection, built on the MMDetection toolbox. It reproduces the Grounding-DINO architecture, which uses a Swin Transformer image backbone and BERT text encoder with a cross-modality decoder, while replacing the proprietary Cap4M pre-training dataset with GRIT and V3Det. The model is trained on 15 datasets covering Open-Vocabulary Detection, Phrase Grounding, and Referring Expression Comprehension. In zero-shot evaluation, MM-Grounding-DINO-Tiny achieves 50.6 mAP on COCO and 41.4 AP on LVIS mini, outperforming the original Grounding-DINO-Tiny by 2.2 and 12.6 points respectively. Fine-tuning on COCO yields 58.2 mAP after 12 epochs. A limitation is that the GRIT dataset contains noisy annotations, including abstract phrases and full-image bounding boxes, which provides limited benefit for standard detection tasks compared to V3Det.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Grounding-DINO's training code is unreleased, so the authors rebuild it in MMDetection and extend benchmarks for three grounding tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Approach
digest_headlines.headline: Grounding-DINO's cross-modality architecture is kept, with a bias added to the contrastive embedding and random negative samples in augmentation.

digest_headlines.heading: Main Results
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot tests show the Tiny variants beat Grounding-DINO-Tiny on detection and referring-expression benchmarks, with the largest gains on the long-tail benchmark.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude the open pipeline matches or beats the Grounding-DINO baseline and release it as a shared resource.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix adds threshold sweeps, per-dataset tables for three benchmarks, open-vocabulary fine-tuning results and failure-case visualizations.

repos.title: Unlimited OCR Works
repos.paper_summary: Unlimited OCR is a decoder change to DeepSeek OCR that replaces every decoder attention layer with Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA). Each output token attends to all prefix tokens (visual tokens and the prompt) plus the preceding 128 output tokens, so the KV cache is bounded by prefix length plus 128 rather than growing with output length. The model is continued from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps on about 2M document samples, with the DeepEncoder frozen and 32K-token training sequences. On OmniDocBench v1.5, the overall score rises from 87.01 (DeepSeek OCR) to 93.23. On v1.6, it reaches 93.92, the highest overall score in that table. Decoding throughput is 5580 versus 4951 tokens/s (12.7% higher) at 512 concurrency, measured on short OmniDocBench pages. The paper states that prefill still grows with page count, so the 32K context limits how many pages fit in one pass; the authors plan 128K training.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current OCR models cannot parse ten pages in one pass, so the paper proposes constant-memory attention for long-horizon parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior end-to-end OCR decoders grow their KV cache with output length, which limits speed and length, so the paper builds on DeepSeek OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Reference Sliding Window Attention lets each token see all visual and prompt tokens plus the preceding 128 output tokens, keeping the cache constant.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Settings
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses about 2 million document samples, with synthetic multi-page data, and continues from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR scores 93.23 on OmniDocBench v1.5, above DeepSeek OCR's 87.01, and 93.92 on v1.6.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficiency Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: At 6,000 tokens, DeepSeek OCR's generation speed falls 35% behind Unlimited OCR, which keeps a stable rate as output grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitation and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR is not truly unlimited because prefill length still grows with page count, so the authors plan longer contexts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Replacing all decoder attention with R-SWA leaves parsing performance lossless, and the authors expect wider use beyond OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Author List
digest_headlines.headline: Lists the core contributors and contributors to the Unlimited OCR report, marking the project leader and technical director.

repos.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
repos.paper_summary: Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting is a zero-shot prompting strategy for large language models that instructs the model to devise a plan dividing a task into subtasks before executing them. The extended variant, PS+, adds instructions to extract relevant variables and calculate intermediate results. On ten datasets covering arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning using GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT by an average of 6.3% on arithmetic tasks, reaching 76.7% accuracy compared to 70.4%. It also exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought on five of six arithmetic benchmarks. Error analysis on GSM8K shows PS+ reduces calculation errors from 7% to 5% and missing-step errors from 12% to 7%, though semantic misunderstanding errors remain at 27%. The paper notes two limitations: prompt sensitivity requires careful manual design, and the method does not address semantic understanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

digest_headlines.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
digest_headlines.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics
digest_headlines.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.

repos.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
LLaMA is a series of open-source foundation language models with 7B to 65B parameters, trained on 1.4T tokens from publicly available datasets. The architecture uses RMSNorm, SwiGLU activations, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). Training employed the AdamW optimizer with a cosine learning rate schedule.

On zero-shot common sense reasoning benchmarks, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most tasks, while LLaMA-65B surpasses Chinchilla-70B on all but BoolQ. For closed-book question answering, LLaMA-65B achieves 23.8% exact match on NaturalQuestions in the zero-shot setting, comparable to PaLM-540B. On GSM8k mathematical reasoning, LLaMA-65B scores 50.9%, exceeding Minerva-62B despite lacking math-specific fine-tuning. In code generation, LLaMA-65B achieves a pass@1 score of 23.7% on HumanEval, matching PaLM-62B.

A limitation is that LLaMA-65B trails Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B on MMLU by several percent, likely due to using less book data (177 GB) than competitors. Additionally, toxicity scores increase with model size, reaching 0.141 for LLaMA-65B on respectful prompts.

repos.title: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Step-DPO is a preference optimization method for large language models that treats individual reasoning steps, rather than full answers, as the unit of comparison to improve mathematical reasoning. The method modifies the standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective by conditioning on preceding correct steps and optimizing the probability of the next correct step versus the first erroneous step. This allows the model to pinpoint specific errors in long chains of thought without penalizing earlier correct logic.

The authors construct a dataset of 10K preference pairs using a three-step pipeline: collecting incorrect model outputs, localizing the first error, and sampling self-generated corrections from the reference model. They find that using in-distribution data generated by the model itself yields better results than out-of-distribution data written by humans or GPT-4. On the MATH benchmark, applying Step-DPO to Qwen2-72B-Instruct increases accuracy from 69.4% to 70.8%, while GSM8K accuracy rises from 92.4% to 94.0%. These gains are achieved with fewer than 500 training steps. The approach also improves performance on competition-level problems like AIME 2024, where Qwen2-72B-Instruct scores 4/30 compared to 5/30 for the base instruct model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Step-DPO
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.

repos.title: Monocular Identity-Conditioned Facial Reflectance Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: ID2Reflectance is a framework for monocular facial reflectance reconstruction that estimates diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness, and surface normal maps from a single in-the-wild image. The method learns a facial prior in image space rather than UV space to reduce dependency on limited light-stage data. It trains a VQGAN with multi-domain codebooks, aligning RGB and reflectance domains by jointly training on FFHQ and 135 captured subjects. An identity-conditioned swapper module, trained on VGGFace2HQ using AdaIN, injects identity features from the target image into the pre-trained decoder. At inference, the system synthesizes three-view reflectance images and stitches them into UV-space maps. On a test set of 20 subjects, ID2Reflectance achieves a PSNR of 28.47 dB for diffuse albedo, outperforming TRUST (21.63 dB) and ID2Albedo (23.72 dB). Identity similarity reaches 0.735 compared to 0.532 for ID2Albedo. The total inference time is 3.8 seconds per face on an A6000 GPU. The paper notes that reconstructed PBR maps may not be physically plausible due to the lack of ground-truth supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reflectance models trained on few light-stage captures generalize poorly, so the method learns the reflectance prior in image space from abundant RGB faces.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior facial reflectance methods depend on light-stage data and their data is unreleased, while face swapping methods target only the RGB domain.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Two-stage codebook training aligns reflectance with RGB, so identity swapping learned on RGB transfers to reflectance maps.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Trained on 115 captured subjects, the method gives identity-preserved reflectance on Digital Emily and in-the-wild faces in 3.8 seconds/face.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that limited captured data yields a reliable reflectance prior and notes the method could be misused.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the light stage rig, public datasets, codebook and swapper details, UV stitching, a fairness benchmark, and further qualitative results.

repos.title: LeRobot: An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary:
`lerobot` is an open-source Python library for end-to-end robot learning that integrates low-level motor control, data collection, and policy training. It supports eight hardware platforms, including the SO-100 and ALOHA-2, using a shared middleware API for teleoperation. The library introduces `LeRobotDataset`, a standardized format for multimodal robotics data that enables streaming large datasets without full downloads. As of September 2025, the ecosystem includes over 16,000 datasets from 2,200 contributors.

The library provides PyTorch implementations of leading algorithms such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0}$, and SmolVLA. Inference benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 show ACT achieving 5.01 ms latency, while the larger $\pi_{0}$ model requires 209 ms. An asynchronous inference stack decouples action prediction from execution, allowing policies to run on remote machines. Limitations include incomplete coverage of robot embodiments and algorithms, and the lack of low-level optimizations like quantization or graph compilation for practical deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robot learning tools are fragmented, so the authors present lerobot, an open-source library spanning the full stack from motor control to datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and this accessibility supports decentralized data collection.

digest_headlines.heading: Features
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot supports several low-cost arms, a shared dataset format with 16K+ datasets, and reference implementations of policies.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation is used only for benchmarking, since the authors find simulation challenging for the contact-rich tasks the library targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot is presented as a unified open stack, with limits in robot coverage, algorithm count, and inference optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists robot build guides, dataset breakdowns, the streaming dataset design, model and inference examples, and a synchronous versus asynchronous comparison.

repos.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
repos.paper_summary: FlashAttention is an exact attention algorithm that reduces GPU memory traffic by tiling the computation to avoid materializing the full $N \times N$ attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). It computes softmax incrementally over blocks of keys and values loaded into on-chip SRAM, storing only normalization statistics for the backward pass. The paper proves FlashAttention requires $\Theta(N^2 d^2 M^{-1})$ HBM accesses, where $d$ is head dimension and $M$ is SRAM size, compared to $\Theta(Nd + N^2)$ for standard attention, establishing a lower bound showing no exact algorithm can asymptotically improve this for all $M$. On GPT-2 with sequence length 1024, it achieves a 7.6x speedup over PyTorch attention. End-to-end training yields a 15% speedup on BERT-large versus MLPerf 1.1 records, a 3x speedup on GPT-2 versus HuggingFace baselines, and a 2.4x speedup on Long-Range Arena. Longer contexts enabled by FlashAttention improve GPT-2 perplexity by 0.7 and achieve better-than-chance accuracy on Path-X (61.4%) and Path-256 (63.1%). Limitations include the need for custom CUDA kernels for each new attention variant and lack of support for multi-GPU IO optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Attention is quadratic in sequence length, and making it IO-aware reduces slow GPU memory accesses while keeping results exact.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: GPU attention is memory-bound, and standard attention writes the N by N score and probability matrices to HBM.

digest_headlines.heading: FlashAttention: Algorithm, Analysis, and Extensions
digest_headlines.headline: Tiling and recomputation give exact attention with fewer HBM accesses, and a lower bound limits any exact algorithm.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: FlashAttention trains BERT-large 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record and GPT-2 up to 3x faster than HuggingFace.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Limitations are that each attention variant needs its own low-level GPU kernel and that multi-GPU data transfer is not analyzed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, backward-pass derivations, algorithm details, proofs, extensions and full benchmark tables.
